# Mahādukkhakkhandha Sutta (MN 13 (PTS MN i 83))

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mahādukkhakkhandha Sutta* ("The Longer Discourse on the Mass of Suffering" [SuttaCentral]; also rendered "The Greater Discourse on the Mass of Suffering" [Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995]) is the thirteenth discourse of the Majjhimanikāya. Prompted by non-Buddhist wanderers who claim their teaching is identical to that of the Buddha, the discourse sets out to demonstrate that other ascetics lack genuine comprehension of sensual pleasures, material form, and feelings [SuttaCentral; Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995]. The sutta is systematically organized around the threefold analysis of gratification (*assāda*), danger (*ādīnava*), and escape (*nissaraṇa*) [Radich 2007; Anālayo 2014]. In expounding the dangers of sensual indulgence, the Buddha depicts physical pain and bodily affliction in vivid detail [Radich 2007] and demonstrates how craving for sensual gratification directly generates competition, criminality, and warfare [Anālayo 2014]. In the analysis of material form, the sutta contrasts the transient beauty of youth with the progressive stages of a decaying corpse in a charnel ground to reveal bodily impermanence and disadvantage [Anālayo 2014; Radich 2007].

The text has full parallels in the Chinese *Madhyama-āgama* (MĀ 99) and the *Ekottarika-āgama* (EĀ 21.9), as well as an early individual Chinese translation, the *Kuyin jing* (苦陰經, T 53) [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral and DharmaNexus both confirm that MN 13 shares extensive textual material with the Pali *Cūḷadukkhakkhandha Sutta* (MN 14), specifically MN 13 §§7–15 coinciding with MN 14 §§6–14 [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus; Nattier 2008]. Substantial internal reuse is also shared with the *Khaggavisāṇasuttaniddesa* (Cnd 23) and portions of the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* (AN 10, AN 4) and *Saṁyutta Nikāya* (SN 46, SN 36) [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus additionally aligns passages of the text with Sanskrit treatises such as Śāntideva's *Śikṣāsamuccaya* and the *Śrāvakabhūmi* [DharmaNexus]. Commenting on MN 13, the *Papañcasūdanī* (Ps II 54) explains the "full understanding of sensual pleasures" (*kāmānaṁ pariññā*) as implying their eradication (*pahāna*) [Anālayo 2011]. On linguistic grounds, Kingsbury's study of aorist forms places MN 13 in the middle chronological stratum of canonical discourses [Radich 2007].
